# 4 Benchmarks

## BENCHMARKS {#a}

Measuring the return of a portfolio in isolation provides only part of the story; we need to know if the return is good or bad. In other words, we need to evaluate performance (risk and return), against an appropriate benchmark.

Benchmark is defined in the *Oxford English Dictionary* as "a standard or point of reference against which things may be compared". Not readily translated into other languages, it derives from a surveyor's mark cut in a wall and used as a reference point in measuring altitudes.

### Benchmark attributes {#b}

Good benchmarks should have the following attributes:

**(1) *Appropriate***

The chosen benchmark must be relevant to the appropriate investment strategy. It is essential that the benchmark matches the asset owner's requirements.

**(2) *Investable***

The asset manager should be able to invest in all the securities included in the benchmark. If not, there will always be an element of relative performance for which the asset manager has no control.

**(3) *Accessible***

To allow the asset manager to construct the portfolio relative to the benchmark it is essential that there is access not only to the return information of the benchmark but the constituent elements and their weights at the start of the period of measurement.

**(4) *Independent***

An independent third party should construct and calculate all benchmark returns to ensure a fair comparison.

### Best benchmark practice {#c}

I draw a distinction between the design of a good benchmark and best practice in the use of that benchmark. Benchmarks should be:

**(1) *Unambiguous***

The chosen benchmark should be clear, well documented and unambiguous. It is bad performance measurement practice to measure performance against more than one benchmark and to change benchmarks retrospectively.

**(2) *Specified in advance***

The chosen benchmark should be determined in advance (ex-ante) of the measurement period.

**(3) *Never retrospectively changed***

The chosen benchmark should not be retrospectively changed (ex-post). It is clearly inappropriate to deliver performance against an agreed benchmark, and if underperforming to search for an alternative benchmark against which the portfolio can demonstrate apparent outperformance.

> **Note**
>
> Bailey, Richards and Tierney (Bailey, Richards and Tierney, "Benchmark Portfolios and the Manager/Plan Sponsor Relationship" (1988).) combined both good attributes and best practice in their description of "properties of a valid benchmark":
>
> *Unambiguous* – The names and weights of securities comprising the benchmark are clearly delineated.
>
> *Investable* – The option is available to forgo active management and simply hold the benchmark.
>
> *Measurable* – The benchmark's return can be readily calculated on a reasonably frequent basis.
>
> *Appropriate* – The benchmark is consistent with the manager's investment style.
>
> *Reflective of current investment opinions* – The manager has current investment knowledge (be it positive, negative or neutral) regarding the securities that constitute the benchmark.
>
> *Specified in advance* – The benchmark is constructed prior to the start of an evaluation period.
>
> *Accountable* – The manager accepts ownership and accountability for the composition and performance of the benchmark.
